questions.stem: A 63 year old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease has 6 months of aching hips and difficulty rising from a chair. He eats a varied diet and walks outdoors daily. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.08 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), ALP 196 U/L (30–130), PTH 28 pmol/L (1.6–8.5), 25-OH vitamin D 72 nmol/L (>50), 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D low, eGFR 18 mL/min.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying cause of his osteomalacia?
questions.e: Normal 25-OH vitamin D with low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D means the kidney cannot activate vitamin D: CKD-related osteomalacia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Storage form normal, **active** form low, kidneys failing.

elim: He takes no anticonvulsants.
Malabsorption would lower 25-OH vitamin D.
His diet is varied and 25-OH vitamin D is normal.
He is outdoors daily and 25-OH vitamin D is normal.

steps.x: **B. Chronic kidney disease.** Causes: low UV, CKD, malabsorption, anticonvulsants.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman of Pakistani heritage has 9 months of aching in her pelvis, thighs and ribs. She dresses fully covered and works indoors. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 114/72 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Dark skin and little sun exposure with diffuse bone pain, low calcium and phosphate, raised ALP and PTH and very low vitamin D is osteomalacia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.

clues: dresses fully covered and works indoors
aching in her pelvis, thighs and ribs
steps.x: Darker skin, **no sunlight**, diffuse symmetrical bone aches.

elim: Fibromyalgia has normal bloods.
Her TSH is normal.
Osteoporosis is painless until fracture and has a normal bone profile.
Primary disease has a high, not low, calcium.

steps.x: **C. Osteomalacia.** Low vitamin D + low calcium/phosphate + high ALP + high PTH = osteomalacia.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man who has been housebound with agoraphobia for 3 years has diffuse bone pain and weakness of his thighs. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Diffuse bone pain, proximal weakness and a raised bone ALP (normal GGT) is the signature triad of osteomalacia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
**Bone pain + proximal weakness + raised ALP** with low calcium and phosphate.

elim: Myeloma raises calcium and keeps ALP normal.
Paget's is focal, with normal calcium and phosphate.
Polymyositis raises creatine kinase; his is normal.
Metastases rarely lower both calcium and phosphate at 49.

steps.x: **B. Osteomalacia.** Signature triad: bone pain, proximal weakness, raised ALP.

questions.stem: A 78 year old woman in a care home has 3 weeks of groin pain without any fall. X-ray shows an undisplaced insufficiency fracture of the left pubic ramus. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 132/78 mmHg. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.14 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (0.80–1.50), ALP 188 U/L (30–130), 25-OH vitamin D 14 nmol/L (>50).
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
questions.e: Soft, poorly mineralised bone fractures without trauma; abnormal bone biochemistry with low vitamin D separates osteomalacia from osteoporosis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Housebound, **atraumatic** fracture, abnormal bone profile.

elim: Metastases do not cause low calcium, low phosphate and low vitamin D.
OA does not cause fractures or this bone profile.
Osteoporosis has a normal calcium, phosphate and ALP.
Paget's has normal calcium and phosphate.

steps.x: **C. Osteomalacia.** Osteoporosis has normal bloods; osteomalacia does not.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman who moved to the UK from Afghanistan has years of bone pain and her legs have become increasingly bowed. She has always eaten little dairy and rarely goes outdoors. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.06 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 0.66 mmol/L (0.80–1.50), ALP 256 U/L (30–130), 25-OH vitamin D 9 nmol/L (>50).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Defective mineralisation leaves bones soft, so they bow under load; with very low vitamin D and a raised ALP this is osteomalacia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.

clues: little dairy and rarely goes outdoors
steps.x: Soft bones **bending** in a woman with severe vitamin D deficiency.

elim: Achondroplasia is congenital short-limbed dwarfism with normal bloods.
Hypophosphatasia also softens bone but has a LOW ALP.
OI causes fractures and blue sclerae with normal bloods.
Osteoporosis does not bow bones or change the bone profile.

steps.x: **D. Osteomalacia.** Osteomalacia: soft bones, pain, fractures, deformity.

questions.stem: A 2 year old girl is brought to the GP because her legs have bowed since she started walking. She was exclusively breastfed until 18 months and has dark skin. She has thickened wrists and bumps along her ribs. Investigations: calcium low, phosphate low, ALP 980 U/L (raised for age), 25-OH vitamin D 8 nmol/L (>50).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Vitamin D deficiency before epiphyseal fusion causes rickets, the childhood equivalent of osteomalacia: bowed legs, widened wrists and a rachitic rosary.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.

clues: thickened wrists and bumps along her ribs
steps.x: Defective mineralisation in a child with **open growth plates**.

elim: Blount disease is a growth plate problem with normal bloods.
Fractures with normal bloods; this is a metabolic bone disease.
OI has normal calcium, phosphate and vitamin D.
Physiological bowing has normal bloods and no wrist or rib signs.

steps.x: **E. Rickets.** Osteomalacia in children (before epiphyseal fusion) = rickets.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 6 years ago and has not attended follow-up. She now has aching ribs and hips and struggles to climb stairs. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.09 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 0.71 mmol/L (0.80–1.50), ALP 204 U/L (30–130), 25-OH vitamin D 15 nmol/L (>50), eGFR >90 mL/min.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her osteomalacia?
questions.e: Gastric bypass reduces absorption of vitamin D and calcium, a malabsorption cause of osteomalacia, like coeliac disease.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Bypass surgery means **malabsorption** of fat-soluble vitamin D.

elim: She takes no anticonvulsants.
Her eGFR is normal.
Primary disease has a high calcium.
This is inherited and presents in childhood with a normal vitamin D.

steps.x: **C. Malabsorption after gastric bypass.** Malabsorption (coeliac, bypass) is a major cause.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has diffuse bone pain and difficulty rising from a chair. Her medicines are carbamazepine, amlodipine, simvastatin, levothyroxine and omeprazole. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.11 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 0.74 mmol/L (0.80–1.50), ALP 186 U/L (30–130), 25-OH vitamin D 18 nmol/L (>50).
questions.q: Which of her medicines is the most likely cause?
questions.e: Enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin) speed vitamin D breakdown in the liver and cause osteomalacia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
An **enzyme-inducing** anticonvulsant.

elim: Calcium channel blockers do not affect vitamin D.
Replacement thyroxine does not cause osteomalacia.
PPIs are linked to low magnesium and fracture, not classic osteomalacia.
Statins cause myopathy but not this bone profile.

steps.x: **B. Carbamazepine.** Anticonvulsants are a classic cause of osteomalacia.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman with vitamin D deficiency has had aching bones for 6 months. She cannot rise from a squat without using her arms. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Her creatine kinase is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Symmetrical proximal weakness with bone tenderness
Unilateral leg weakness with brisk reflexes
questions.e: Osteomalacia gives symmetrical bone tenderness and proximal myopathy; the CK is normal because muscle is not inflamed.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
Hip-girdle weakness plus aching bones, **normal CK**.

elim: That suggests motor neurone disease.
That suggests myasthenia gravis.
That is dermatomyositis, with a raised CK.
That is an upper motor neurone lesion.

steps.x: **D. Symmetrical proximal weakness with bone tenderness.** Osteomalacia: symmetrical bone pain/tenderness + proximal weakness.

questions.stem: A 72 year old housebound man has an ALP of 224 U/L (30–130) on routine bloods. His bilirubin, ALT and GGT are normal. He has aching bones and weak thighs. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. Adjusted calcium is 2.13 mmol/L (2.20–2.60) and 25-OH vitamin D is 11 nmol/L (>50).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his raised ALP?
questions.e: A normal GGT puts the ALP in bone; low calcium and vitamin D with bone pain and weakness is osteomalacia, with ALP raised by increased osteoblast turnover.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.
**Bone** ALP (normal GGT), low calcium and vitamin D.

elim: GGT and bilirubin are normal, so ALP is from bone.
Paget's has a normal calcium and vitamin D.
This raises GGT too.
There is no fracture, and this would not lower calcium.

steps.x: **B. Osteomalacia.** Raised ALP, low calcium, low vitamin D = osteomalacia.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman with long-standing vitamin D deficiency has bone pain and proximal weakness. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg. Renal function is normal. A bone profile with PTH is sent.
questions.q: Which set of results is most likely?
o: High calcium, low phosphate, high ALP, high PTH
Low calcium, high phosphate, normal ALP, low PTH
Low calcium, low phosphate, high ALP, high PTH
Normal calcium, normal phosphate, normal ALP, normal PTH
Normal calcium, normal phosphate, very high ALP, normal PTH
questions.e: Vitamin D deficiency lowers calcium and phosphate; PTH rises in compensation (secondary hyperparathyroidism) and ALP rises with bone turnover.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
Low vitamin D: less calcium and phosphate absorbed, **PTH compensates**.

elim: That is primary hyperparathyroidism.
That is hypoparathyroidism.
That is osteoporosis.
That is Paget's disease.

steps.x: **C. Low calcium, low phosphate, high ALP, high PTH.** Osteomalacia: low Ca, low PO₄, high ALP, high PTH, low vitamin D.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman fractured her wrist after a fall from standing. She is housebound and has had generalised aching for months. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. Her GP wants to know whether she has osteomalacia rather than osteoporosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to distinguish them?
questions.e: Osteomalacia is diagnosed biochemically (low calcium, phosphate and vitamin D, raised ALP and PTH) with supportive imaging; osteoporosis has a normal bone profile and both reduce DEXA density.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
DEXA cannot tell them apart; **biochemistry** can.

elim: Marrow biopsy is for haematological disease.
Both conditions lower bone density on DEXA.
An isotope scan does not separate the two.
MRI shows the fracture but not the cause.

steps.x: **B. Bone profile with 25-OH vitamin D.** Diagnosis = biochemistry + supportive imaging.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man has low calcium, low phosphate, raised ALP and a 25-OH vitamin D of 13 nmol/L (>50). He has groin pain on walking. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. A radiologist is asked where Looser's zones would most typically be seen.
questions.q: Which is the most likely site?
questions.e: Looser's zones (pseudofractures) are lucent transverse lines with sclerotic borders at sites of stress, classically the medial femoral neck (hip), pubic rami and ribs.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
Pseudofractures appear at **stress points** like the hip.

elim: Erosion here suggests hyperparathyroidism.
Skull lesions suggest myeloma or Paget's.
Tuft resorption is a hyperparathyroidism sign.
Vertebral wedge fractures are typical of osteoporosis.

steps.x: **B. Medial femoral neck.** Looser's zones: classically hip (femoral neck), also pubic rami.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has osteomalacia confirmed on bloods. She has had a year of bloating and loose stools, and her ferritin is 6 µg/L (15–150). She eats a normal diet including oily fish. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Her BMI is 18.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to find the underlying cause?
questions.e: Malabsorption with iron deficiency and osteomalacia suggests coeliac disease; anti-tTG IgA is the first test, so the cause can be treated.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
Malabsorption with **iron and vitamin D** deficiency despite a good diet.

elim: Colonoscopy is not the first test for suspected coeliac disease.
Calprotectin screens for IBD, which is less likely.
PTH will be raised but does not reveal the cause.
A year of symptoms is not an acute infection.

steps.x: **A. Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA.** Always look for the cause: coeliac, CKD, drugs, low sunlight.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has bone pain and proximal weakness. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.10 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), ALP 210 U/L (30–130), PTH 34 pmol/L (1.6–8.5), 25-OH vitamin D 68 nmol/L (>50). He has type 2 diabetes and hypertension and takes no anticonvulsants. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 152/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to find the cause?
questions.e: Normal stored vitamin D with features of osteomalacia suggests failed renal activation; diabetes and hypertension make CKD likely.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show or do, then pick it.
Storage vitamin D **normal**: the problem is activation in the kidney.

elim: Malabsorption would lower 25-OH vitamin D.
Myeloma raises calcium.
Calcium is low, so PTH is compensatory.
Thyroid disease does not cause this profile.

steps.x: **E. Urea, creatinine and eGFR.** Osteomalacia with normal 25-OH vitamin D: check renal function.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has osteomalacia due to newly diagnosed coeliac disease confirmed on duodenal biopsy. She has no tetany. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.12 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), 25-OH vitamin D 17 nmol/L (>50).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Gluten-free diet with vitamin D loading
questions.e: Treat both the deficiency (high-dose vitamin D loading) and the underlying cause (a gluten-free diet for coeliac disease).

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Deficiency plus a **treatable cause**.

elim: Bisphosphonates do not correct a mineralisation defect.
Vitamin D must also be replaced.
She has no tetany; IV calcium is for emergencies.
The malabsorption must be treated too, or deficiency recurs.

steps.x: **C. Gluten-free diet with vitamin D loading.** Replace vitamin D and treat the cause.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman has osteomalacia from low sunlight exposure. She drinks no milk and eats no cheese or yoghurt. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.10 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), 25-OH vitamin D 11 nmol/L (>50), eGFR >90 mL/min. She has no tetany.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: First-line treatment is high-dose vitamin D loading; calcium supplements are added when dietary calcium is low.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Severe deficiency, normal kidneys, **low dietary calcium**.

elim: No tetany or seizures.
Vitamin D must be replaced to absorb calcium.
Active vitamin D is for CKD or hypoparathyroidism; her kidneys are normal.
This is a maintenance dose, too low for deficiency.

steps.x: **A. Colecalciferol loading plus calcium supplements.** High-dose colecalciferol loading, plus calcium if intake is low.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has completed a 7 week colecalciferol loading course for osteomalacia. Her bone pain has eased. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. 25-OH vitamin D is now 74 nmol/L (>50). She works night shifts and asks how to stop it coming back.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term advice?
o: Maintenance low-dose vitamin D daily with safe sunlight and diet
questions.e: After loading, maintenance with low-dose vitamin D (400 to 800 IU daily) plus sunlight and diet optimisation prevents recurrence.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.

clues: completed a 7 week colecalciferol loading course
how to stop it coming back
steps.x: Loaded and better, but still **low sunlight**.

elim: Repeated loading is not standard; daily maintenance is.
Sunlight helps make vitamin D.
Active vitamin D is not needed with normal kidneys.
Her risk factors persist, so deficiency would recur.

steps.x: **D. Maintenance low-dose vitamin D daily with safe sunlight and diet.** Maintenance: 400–800 IU daily + lifestyle.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman with severe osteomalacia has a generalised seizure in clinic that stops after 2 minutes. She has no history of epilepsy. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm, BP 128/80 mmHg and glucose 5.4 mmol/L. Investigations: adjusted calcium 1.62 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), magnesium 0.82 mmol/L (0.70–1.00).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
questions.e: Severe hypocalcaemia causing seizures or tetany is an emergency: correct urgently with IV calcium gluconate, then replace vitamin D.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Hypocalcaemic **seizure**: emergency.

elim: The seizure was provoked by hypocalcaemia; treat the cause.
Her magnesium is normal.
Too slow for a seizure.
Vitamin D takes weeks; correct calcium first.

steps.x: **A. IV calcium gluconate.** Tetany or seizures: urgent IV calcium.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease has bone pain and proximal weakness. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.06 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), PTH 31 pmol/L (1.6–8.5), 25-OH vitamin D 70 nmol/L (>50), low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. His phosphate is controlled with a binder. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 144/86 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.e: In CKD the kidney cannot 1-alpha-hydroxylate vitamin D, so an active analogue such as alfacalcidol is given, with renal input.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Storage vitamin D fine, **activation** has failed.

elim: His stored vitamin D is normal; his kidneys cannot activate it.
He has no tetany or seizures.
Bisphosphonates do not correct defective mineralisation and are used cautiously in CKD.
His PTH is a compensatory response.

steps.x: **A. Alfacalcidol.** CKD osteomalacia: active vitamin D (alfacalcidol).

questions.stem: A 38 year old man with epilepsy, well controlled on phenytoin for 15 years, has osteomalacia. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.14 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), ALP 178 U/L (30–130), 25-OH vitamin D 16 nmol/L (>50). His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. He has had no seizures for 10 years.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Vitamin D loading then maintenance, continuing phenytoin
questions.e: Replace vitamin D with a loading course then maintenance; any change of anticonvulsant is a specialist decision, never abrupt.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Drug-induced deficiency in **well-controlled epilepsy**.

elim: His kidneys are normal, and stopping an anticonvulsant risks seizures.
Bisphosphonates do not correct a mineralisation defect.
Abrupt withdrawal risks seizures.
Deficiency needs a loading dose first.

steps.x: **D. Vitamin D loading then maintenance, continuing phenytoin.** Load, then maintain; do not stop anticonvulsants abruptly.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman has started high-dose colecalciferol loading for osteomalacia. Her adjusted calcium before treatment was 2.18 mmol/L (2.20–2.60). Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg. She asks what follow-up bloods she needs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate monitoring?
o: Adjusted calcium about 1 month after loading
questions.e: Calcium is checked about a month after loading, because vitamin D can unmask primary hyperparathyroidism and cause hypercalcaemia.

steps.x: A management question: decide what this patient needs at this moment.
Loading can **unmask** hypercalcaemia.

elim: Weekly levels are unnecessary.
Bone density changes slowly.
Loading can unmask hypercalcaemia.
Weekly PTH does not guide treatment.

steps.x: **B. Adjusted calcium about 1 month after loading.** Check calcium 1 month after vitamin D loading.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has osteomalacia from dietary vitamin D deficiency and little sunlight. Her adjusted calcium is 2.10 mmol/L (2.20–2.60) and phosphate 0.70 mmol/L (0.80–1.50). A student asks why vitamin D deficiency lowers both minerals.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Increased renal calcium excretion caused by PTH
Reduced dietary intake of calcium alone
Reduced intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption
questions.e: Active vitamin D drives gut absorption of calcium and phosphate; without it both fall and osteoid cannot mineralise.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Vitamin D's main job: absorb calcium and phosphate **from the gut**.

elim: Calcitonin plays little part in human calcium balance.
PTH increases renal calcium reabsorption.
Bone resorption increases with secondary hyperparathyroidism.
This does not explain low phosphate or the vitamin D link.

steps.x: **E. Reduced intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption.** Low vitamin D → less gut calcium and phosphate → poor mineralisation.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man with osteomalacia has an iliac crest bone biopsy. The pathologist compares it with a biopsy from a woman with postmenopausal osteoporosis. A student asks how the two differ.
questions.q: Which best describes the bone in osteomalacia?
o: Brittle bone from defective type 1 collagen
Disorganised woven bone with mosaic pattern
Normal matrix volume with impaired hydroxyapatite deposition
Reduced bone mass with normal mineralisation
Replacement of marrow by plasma cells
questions.e: In osteomalacia low calcium and phosphate stop hydroxyapatite being laid down, leaving excess unmineralised osteoid and soft bone; osteoporosis has less bone that is normally mineralised.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Osteomalacia is a **mineralisation** defect, not a loss of bone mass.

elim: That is osteogenesis imperfecta.
That is Paget's disease.
That is osteoporosis.
That is myeloma.

steps.x: **C. Normal matrix volume with impaired hydroxyapatite deposition.** Osteomalacia = soft (unmineralised); osteoporosis = thin (normal mineral).

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman with osteomalacia has an adjusted calcium of 2.15 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), PTH of 15.2 pmol/L (1.6–8.5) and phosphate of 0.62 mmol/L (0.80–1.50). Her calcium is only slightly low despite a 25-OH vitamin D of 10 nmol/L (>50).
questions.q: Which best explains her raised PTH?
questions.e: Low calcium stimulates PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism), which resorbs bone to hold calcium up, wastes phosphate and drives the raised ALP.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Glands responding to **low calcium**; they keep it nearly normal.

elim: An adenoma would raise calcium.
That is pseudohypoparathyroidism, with high phosphate.
Her phosphate is low.
Tertiary disease has a high calcium.

steps.x: **B. Compensatory response to hypocalcaemia.** Secondary hyperparathyroidism is a compensation in osteomalacia.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man with osteomalacia has an ALP of 246 U/L (30–130) with a normal GGT. A student asks why ALP is raised when the bone is poorly mineralised.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Increased osteoblast activity driven by secondary hyperparathyroidism
questions.e: Secondary hyperparathyroidism increases bone turnover, and active osteoblasts trying to mineralise osteoid release ALP.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Bone ALP comes from **osteoblasts**; PTH has stepped up turnover.

elim: GGT is normal, so ALP is from bone.
ALP is made by osteoblasts, not osteoclasts.
That is myeloma, where ALP is normal.
ALP is not cleared by the kidney in this way.

steps.x: **B. Increased osteoblast activity driven by secondary hyperparathyroidism.** High PTH → high turnover → high ALP.

questions.stem: A 51 year old woman with osteomalacia has a pelvic X-ray showing bilateral narrow lucent bands at right angles to the cortex of the pubic rami, with sclerotic margins. There is no history of trauma.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for these lines?
o: Focal unmineralised osteoid at sites of mechanical stress
questions.e: Looser's zones are pseudofractures: bands of unmineralised osteoid at sites of stress, seen as lucent transverse lines with sclerotic borders.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.

clues: narrow lucent bands at right angles to the cortex
steps.x: Symmetrical **pseudofractures** with no trauma.

elim: There was no trauma, and they are symmetrical.
Myeloma lesions are round punched-out lucencies.
Metastases are dense, not lucent bands.
That is a hyperparathyroidism sign in the phalanges.

steps.x: **A. Focal unmineralised osteoid at sites of mechanical stress.** Looser's zones = unmineralised osteoid at stress sites.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman with osteomalacia could not climb stairs without help. After 3 months of vitamin D replacement, her thigh strength has returned to normal. Her creatine kinase was normal throughout and nerve conduction studies were normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her recovery?
o: Restored vitamin D receptor signalling in skeletal muscle
questions.e: Skeletal muscle has vitamin D receptors; deficiency impairs muscle protein synthesis and function, causing proximal weakness that improves with replacement.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.
Weakness without myositis or neuropathy, **reversed** by vitamin D.

elim: Recovery of strength is from muscle, not fracture healing.
Nerve conduction was normal.
CK was normal, so there was no myositis.
She was not on steroids.

steps.x: **D. Restored vitamin D receptor signalling in skeletal muscle.** Proximal myopathy in osteomalacia = muscle vitamin D receptor deficiency.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy has bowed legs and widened wrists from vitamin D deficiency. His 30 year old mother has bone pain and proximal weakness from the same cause, but her bones have not changed shape at the ends. A student asks why the conditions look different.
questions.q: Which best explains the difference?
o: Children absorb more vitamin D than adults
Rickets affects growth plates before epiphyseal fusion
Rickets is caused by excess PTH alone
questions.e: The same mineralisation defect in children, before the epiphyses fuse, disrupts growth plates (rickets); in adults it causes osteomalacia.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding with the underlying mechanism.

clues: her bones have not changed shape at the ends
steps.x: Child has **open growth plates**; adult does not.

elim: Absorption does not explain the different features.
Both are due to vitamin D deficiency here.
Osteomalacia affects the whole skeleton.
PTH rises in both as compensation.

steps.x: **D. Rickets affects growth plates before epiphyseal fusion.** Rickets = osteomalacia before epiphyseal fusion.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman who follows a strict vegan diet and rarely goes outdoors has 2 months of foot pain. X-ray shows an insufficiency fracture of the third metatarsal, although she does not run or exercise. She also has aching thighs. Her BMI is 22 and her periods are regular. Investigations: adjusted calcium 2.12 mmol/L (2.20–2.60), phosphate 0.71 mmol/L (0.80–1.50), ALP 192 U/L (30–130).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A low-trauma insufficiency fracture with low calcium and phosphate and raised ALP in someone with little sunlight and no dietary vitamin D is osteomalacia.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.

clues: strict vegan diet and rarely goes outdoors
steps.x: **Insufficiency** fracture without overuse, abnormal bone profile, two risk factors.

elim: Her BMI is normal, periods are regular and osteoporosis has a normal bone profile.
Hypothyroidism does not cause fractures with this bone profile.
Reactive arthritis inflames joints and does not fracture bone.
She does not run or exercise.

steps.x: **E. Vitamin D-deficient osteomalacia.** Insufficiency fractures with abnormal bone biochemistry: osteomalacia.

questions.stem: An 81 year old woman who lives alone and rarely leaves her flat has had four falls in 2 months. She has no dizziness and her lying and standing BP are 132/78 and 130/76 mmHg. She needs to push up with her arms to stand and walks with a waddling gait. Her 25-OH vitamin D is 8 nmol/L (>50) and ALP 210 U/L (30–130).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her falls?
questions.e: Vitamin D deficiency causes a proximal myopathy with a waddling gait and difficulty rising, a common and reversible cause of falls in housebound older people.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern before looking at the options.

clues: push up with her arms to stand
steps.x: Proximal weakness and **waddling gait** with very low vitamin D.

elim: She has no dizziness.
A waddling gait with proximal weakness is not cerebellar ataxia.
Her lying and standing BP are the same.
Parkinson's gives a shuffling, not waddling, gait.

steps.x: **E. Proximal myopathy due to osteomalacia.** Housebound faller with a waddling gait: check vitamin D.
